claim: Pterosaurs were the first vertebrates to achieve powered flight.
source: Pterosaurs were the first vertebrates to achieve powered flight (Palmer, 2017).

claim: Early pterosaurs had long stiff tails with a mobile base that could shift their center of mass.
source: Early pterosaurs had long stiff tails with a mobile base that could shift their center of mass, potentially benefiting flight control.
evidence: Stated in abstract as established fact

claim: The first pterosaurs, the non-pterodactyloids, had long, stiff tails with a mobile base.
source: The first pterosaurs, the non-pterodactyloids, had long, stiff tails with a mobile base (Frey et al., 2003), similar to some dinosaurs like Velociraptor (Persons and Currie, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frey et al., 2003 and Persons and Currie, 2012

claim: Many pterosaur tails end in a soft tissue 'vane'.
source: Many of these tails end in a soft tissue 'vane' (Marsh, 1882; Döderlein, 1929; Frey et al., 2003; Figure 1), which may have contributed to passive stability in flight.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1

claim: The tail vane may have contributed to passive stability in flight.
source: Many of these tails end in a soft tissue 'vane' (Marsh, 1882; Döderlein, 1929; Frey et al., 2003; Figure 1), which may have contributed to passive stability in flight.

claim: A primary role in display has been suggested for the tail vane.
source: A primary role in display has also been suggested (O'Brien et al., 2018), given ontogenetic shape changes in the vane and the fact that, unlike most aircraft, flying animals do not need vertical control surfaces to be yaw-stable during turns (Bowers, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Brien et al., 2018 and Bowers, 2016

claim: Flying animals do not need vertical control surfaces to be yaw-stable during turns.
source: A primary role in display has also been suggested (O'Brien et al., 2018), given ontogenetic shape changes in the vane and the fact that, unlike most aircraft, flying animals do not need vertical control surfaces to be yaw-stable during turns (Bowers, 2016).

claim: The vanes have been interpreted as steering aids.
source: The vanes have been interpreted as steering aids (Frey et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frey et al., 2003

claim: The length and stiffening of the tails suggest that they might have been important in early pterosaurs for control based on mass shifting or inertial control.
source: The length and stiffening of the tails suggest that they might have been important in early pterosaurs for control based on mass shifting or inertial control, as purported for terrestrial theropods with convergent tails (Persons and Currie, 2012).
evidence: Inference supported by citation to Persons and Currie, 2012

claim: Vane fluttering would be extremely costly and destabilising unless the vane was tensioned while under aerodynamic load.
source: However, vane fluttering would be extremely costly and destabilising unless the vane was tensioned while under aerodynamic load.
evidence: Based on biomechanical principles and knowledge of aerodynamics

claim: Tail vanes feature thick, evenly spaced, internal structures roughly perpendicular to the caudal series.
source: Tail vanes feature thick, evenly spaced, internal structures roughly perpendicular to the caudal series (Döderlein, 1929), that are said to resemble neural spines and haemal arches (Marsh, 1882).
evidence: Supported by citations to Döderlein, 1929 and Marsh, 1882

claim: The internal structures in tail vanes are said to resemble neural spines and haemal arches.
source: Tail vanes feature thick, evenly spaced, internal structures roughly perpendicular to the caudal series (Döderlein, 1929), that are said to resemble neural spines and haemal arches (Marsh, 1882).

claim: The internal structures are presumed to have minimised fluttering and prevented buckling in the same way that spars, ribs, stringers, and longerons do in airplane wings and tail-fins.
source: These structures are presumed to have minimised fluttering and prevented buckling in the same way that spars, ribs, stringers, and longerons do in airplane wings and tail-fins, but others have proposed that they were flexible and cartilaginous (Marsh, 1882), especially since their preserved appearance varies.
evidence: Inference based on engineering principles and comparison to aircraft structures

claim: Others have proposed that the internal structures were flexible and cartilaginous.
source: These structures are presumed to have minimised fluttering and prevented buckling in the same way that spars, ribs, stringers, and longerons do in airplane wings and tail-fins, but others have proposed that they were flexible and cartilaginous (Marsh, 1882), especially since their preserved appearance varies.

claim: Laser-stimulated fluorescence (LSF) imaging was used to investigate the vane's structural properties.
source: Here, we use laser-simulated fluorescence (LSF) imaging of Rhamphorhynchus specimens from the Upper Jurassic Solnhofen Limestones (Kaye et al., 2015; Pittman et al., 2021) to investigate the vane's structural properties, explore its usage, its evolutionary origins and the context for its disappearance in later pterodactyloids (Frey et al., 2003).
evidence: Methodological statement supported by citations to Kaye et al., 2015 and Pittman et al., 2021

claim: The specimens studied are from the Upper Jurassic Solnhofen Limestones.
source: Here, we use laser-simulated fluorescence (LSF) imaging of Rhamphorhynchus specimens from the Upper Jurassic Solnhofen Limestones (Kaye et al., 2015; Pittman et al., 2021) to investigate the vane's structural properties, explore its usage, its evolutionary origins and the context for its disappearance in later pterodactyloids (Frey et al., 2003).

claim: Tail vanes were lost in later pterodactyloids.

evidence: Supported by citation to Frey et al., 2003

claim: Material stiffness is a measure of a material's resistance to deformation and can be summarised by a variable known as the modulus of elasticity (E).
source: Material stiffness is a measure of a material's resistance to deformation and can be summarised by a variable known as the modulus of elasticity (E) which is the ratio of stress (σ) to strain (ϵ) during deformation.

claim: The modulus of elasticity (E) is the ratio of stress (σ) to strain (ϵ) during deformation.
source: Material stiffness is a measure of a material's resistance to deformation and can be summarised by a variable known as the modulus of elasticity (E) which is the ratio of stress (σ) to strain (ϵ) during deformation.

claim: Stress is the applied force divided by the area over which it is exerted.
source: Stress, is the applied force divided by the area over which it is exerted, while strain refers to the change in length of the material: positive strain is stretching (tensile strain) and negative strain is compression (compressive strain).

claim: Strain refers to the change in length of the material.
source: Stress, is the applied force divided by the area over which it is exerted, while strain refers to the change in length of the material: positive strain is stretching (tensile strain) and negative strain is compression (compressive strain).

claim: Positive strain is stretching (tensile strain) and negative strain is compression (compressive strain).
source: Stress, is the applied force divided by the area over which it is exerted, while strain refers to the change in length of the material: positive strain is stretching (tensile strain) and negative strain is compression (compressive strain).

claim: E can differ substantially for different kinds of loading - in soft tissues, resistance to tension is usually much greater than resistance to compression.
source: E can differ substantially for different kinds of loading - in soft tissues, resistance to tension is usually much greater than resistance to compression.

claim: 'True' ligaments running between bones typically only load in tension.
source: For instance, 'true' ligaments running between bones typically only load in tension (i.e. when stretched), they essentially just 'fold up' if compressed (Woo et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Woo et al., 2007

claim: Ligaments essentially just 'fold up' if compressed.
source: For instance, 'true' ligaments running between bones typically only load in tension (i.e. when stretched), they essentially just 'fold up' if compressed (Woo et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Woo et al., 2007

claim: Stiffer materials have a higher value of E than flexible materials.
source: Stiffer materials have a higher value of E than flexible materials: it takes more stress to produce the same strain (they deform less for a given stress).

claim: When the soft tissue surface of the pterosaur wing was placed under aerodynamic load, the associated stress was expected to have stretched the wing surface so it curved towards the side of lower air pressure.
source: When the soft tissue surface of the pterosaur wing was placed under aerodynamic load, the associated stress was expected to have stretched the wing surface so it curved towards the side of lower air pressure.

claim: Wing stretching resulted in 'auto-cambering' of the wing surface, which became more concave beneath (and more convex above).
source: This resulted in 'auto-cambering' of the wing surface, which became more concave beneath (and more convex above).

claim: The degree of auto-cambering was limited by stiffening mechanisms preventing excessive stretching.
source: The degree of auto-cambering was limited by stiffening mechanisms preventing excessive stretching (Palmer and Dyke, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Palmer and Dyke, 2012

claim: Stiffening was provided by a combination of active mechanisms through muscles within the wings as well as passive mechanisms, including keratinisation and reinforcement by fibres within the wing (actinofibrils).
source: Stiffening was provided by a combination of active mechanisms through muscles within the wings as well as passive mechanisms, including keratinisation (stiff keratins have the highest E of any soft tissue) and reinforcement by fibres within the wing (actinofibrils; Palmer and Dyke, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Palmer and Dyke, 2012

claim: Stiff keratins have the highest E of any soft tissue.
source: Stiffening was provided by a combination of active mechanisms through muscles within the wings as well as passive mechanisms, including keratinisation (stiff keratins have the highest E of any soft tissue) and reinforcement by fibres within the wing (actinofibrils; Palmer and Dyke, 2012).

claim: Actinofibrils reinforced the wing against stretching by having a comparatively high value of E in tension.
source: Actinofibrils reinforced the wing against stretching by having a comparatively high value of E in tension: as the entire wing surface bowed, both the ventral and dorsal surfaces were loaded in tension, which applied a tensile load to the actinofibrils.
evidence: Inference based on biomechanical principles and citation to Palmer and Dyke, 2012

claim: As the entire wing surface bowed, both the ventral and dorsal surfaces were loaded in tension.
source: Actinofibrils reinforced the wing against stretching by having a comparatively high value of E in tension: as the entire wing surface bowed, both the ventral and dorsal surfaces were loaded in tension, which applied a tensile load to the actinofibrils.

claim: The actinofibrils stretched according to their elastic modulus in tension, which limited the stretching of the entire wing surface.
source: The actinofibrils stretched according to their elastic modulus in tension, which limited the stretching of the entire wing surface.

claim: The pterosaur tail vane would have experienced asymmetric air flow anytime it was deflected (even slightly) to the right or left during flight.
source: The pterosaur tail vane would have experienced asymmetric air flow anytime it was deflected (even slightly) to the right or left during flight.

claim: Asymmetric air flow would produce a moderate amount of lift, oriented laterally, to either the right or left side depending on the motion of the tail.
source: This would produce a moderate amount of lift, oriented laterally, to either the right or left side depending on the motion of the tail.

claim: The modest lift would have had a tendency to stretch the vane to one side or the other out of plane, much like the auto-cambering of the pterosaur wing.
source: While this modest lift would have been of little use for flight control, it would have had a tendency to stretch the vane to one side or the other out of plane, much like the auto-cambering of the pterosaur wing (Palmer and Dyke, 2012).
evidence: Inference based on aerodynamic principles and citation to Palmer and Dyke, 2012

claim: The rapid stretching and release caused by asymmetric airflow is known as aeroelastic flutter.
source: The associated, rapid, stretching and release this would cause is known as aeroelastic flutter (Lillico et al., 1997), and it produces extremely high drag coefficients.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lillico et al., 1997

claim: Aeroelastic flutter produces extremely high drag coefficients.
source: The associated, rapid, stretching and release this would cause is known as aeroelastic flutter (Lillico et al., 1997), and it produces extremely high drag coefficients.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lillico et al., 1997

claim: Drag on the tail vane would be substantially reduced if the tail vane had a mechanism of tensioning.
source: Drag on the tail vane would therefore be substantially reduced if the tail vane had a mechanism of tensioning.

claim: The lattice of vertical structures and subhorizontal fibres worked as tensile-loaded structures similar to actinofibrils in the wings.
source: We propose that they both worked as tensile-loaded structures similar to actinofibrils in the wings, but acting in tandem due to the lattice cross-links to resist stretching in multiple directions.
evidence: Inference from observational data and biomechanical principles

claim: The lattice structures acted in tandem due to the lattice cross-links to resist stretching in multiple directions.
source: We propose that they both worked as tensile-loaded structures similar to actinofibrils in the wings, but acting in tandem due to the lattice cross-links to resist stretching in multiple directions.
evidence: Inference from observational data and biomechanical principles

claim: The lattice function is analogous to how a fabric with fibres running in multiple directions resists stretching.
source: This is analogous to how a fabric with fibres running in multiple directions resists stretching.

claim: The tail vane would have stretched in the direction of mediolateral deviation.
source: The tail vane would have stretched in the direction of mediolateral deviation.

claim: Since the surface would be stretched, the distances between the lattice fibres would increase - pulling, especially, the thicker vertical structures apart.
source: Since the surface would be stretched, the distances between the lattice fibres would increase - pulling, especially, the thicker vertical structures apart.

claim: These movements would have been limited by both the bending strength of the relatively large vertical 'tubes' and the cross-linking subhorizontal fibres.
source: However, these movements would have been limited by both the bending strength of these relatively large vertical 'tubes' and, more importantly, the cross-linking subhorizontal fibres.
evidence: Inference based on biomechanical principles and observational data

claim: Any stretching of the vane that spread the vertical structures apart from each other would stretch the subhorizontal fibres along their long axis – loading them in tension.
source: Since the subhorizontal fibres linked across the vertical structures, any stretching of the vane that spread the vertical structures apart from each other would stretch the subhorizontal fibres along their long axis – loading them in tension.

claim: This load would ultimately be taken up at the tail tip, where the fibres converged.
source: This load would ultimately be taken up at the tail tip, where the fibres converged.
evidence: Inference based on observational data and biomechanical principles

claim: The concavities along the vane edge being aligned with each structure tip indicates that, under load, the spaces between the structures stretched until the outer edge was linear.
source: This loading regime is consistent with the concavities along the vane edge being aligned with each structure tip, indicating that, under load, the spaces between the structures stretched until the outer edge was linear (Figure 2D), with the fossilised position preserving the unloaded slack condition (Figure 2D).

claim: The fossilised position preserves the unloaded slack condition.
source: This loading regime is consistent with the concavities along the vane edge being aligned with each structure tip, indicating that, under load, the spaces between the structures stretched until the outer edge was linear (Figure 2D), with the fossilised position preserving the unloaded slack condition (Figure 2D).

claim: There is no evidence of active tensioning capacity using muscle in the tail vane.
source: We see no evidence of active tensioning capacity using muscle and therefore posit that this soft tissue lattice was the primary stiffening adaptation for the tail vane.

claim: The soft tissue lattice was the primary stiffening adaptation for the tail vane.
source: We see no evidence of active tensioning capacity using muscle and therefore posit that this soft tissue lattice was the primary stiffening adaptation for the tail vane.

claim: The authors are unaware of any extant organisms with an analogous functional feature to the pterosaur tail vane lattice.
source: We are unaware of any extant organisms with an analogous functional feature.

claim: The precise material composition of the preserved lattice remains elusive.
source: As the precise material composition of the preserved lattice remains elusive, we do not know the absolute value of E for the observed structures, and therefore, cannot calculate expected absolute deflections of the tail vane.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitation in the data

claim: The absolute value of E for the observed structures is not known.
source: As the precise material composition of the preserved lattice remains elusive, we do not know the absolute value of E for the observed structures, and therefore, cannot calculate expected absolute deflections of the tail vane.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitation in the data

claim: Expected absolute deflections of the tail vane cannot be calculated.
source: As the precise material composition of the preserved lattice remains elusive, we do not know the absolute value of E for the observed structures, and therefore, cannot calculate expected absolute deflections of the tail vane.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitation in the data

claim: The presence of the lattice would increase the overall elastic modulus of the tail vane in tension, probably substantially.
source: However, given the orientation and apparent density of the structures, we can confidently predict that the presence of the lattice would increase the overall elastic modulus of the tail vane in tension, probably substantially.
evidence: Inference from observational data and biomechanical principles

claim: Thicker, more condensed collagen fibres can have a tensile E 3.6 times that of thinner, less compact fibres.
source: For perspective, even if all of the observed soft tissue was collagen in life, thicker, more condensed collagen fibres can have a tensile E 3.6 times that of thinner, less compact fibres (Wenger et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wenger et al., 2007

claim: The density and thickness of the structures in the lattice must have been several times that of the surrounding soft tissue matrix to be visibly distinct under LSF.
source: To be visibly distinct under LSF, the density and thickness of the structures in the lattice must have been several times that of the surrounding soft tissue matrix, so it is reasonable to surmise that the lattice could have stiffened the vane by a large margin - probably an order of magnitude, at least.
evidence: Inference from observational data and imaging principles

claim: The lattice could have stiffened the vane by a large margin - probably an order of magnitude, at least.
source: To be visibly distinct under LSF, the density and thickness of the structures in the lattice must have been several times that of the surrounding soft tissue matrix, so it is reasonable to surmise that the lattice could have stiffened the vane by a large margin - probably an order of magnitude, at least.
evidence: Inference from observational data and biomechanical principles

claim: The tail vane maintained effective stiffness dynamically with internal tension of a cross-linked lattice that minimised excessive vane flutter and associated drag production.
source: Thus, our results suggest that the tail vane maintained effective stiffness dynamically with internal tension of a cross-linked lattice that minimised excessive vane flutter and associated drag production.
evidence: Inference from observational data and biomechanical analysis

claim: This structural integrity would have permitted the vane to be an effective display structure without incurring excessive aerodynamic costs.
source: This structural integrity would have permitted the vane to be an effective display structure without incurring excessive aerodynamic costs (Figure 2E).

claim: The tensioning would have allowed the tail, as a whole, to be used for mass-shifting-based aerodynamic control without incurring adverse effects of a fluttering vane during rapid tail motions.
source: This tensioning would also have allowed the tail, as a whole, to be used for mass-shifting-based aerodynamic control without incurring adverse effects of a fluttering vane during rapid tail motions.

claim: Tail vane shape changes through ontogeny.
source: Tail vane shape changes through ontogeny (Bennett, 1995; O'Brien et al., 2018) and between species (Marsh, 1882; Döderlein, 1929; Frey et al., 2003), which underscores the importance of the tail vane in early pterosaur evolution.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett, 1995 and O'Brien et al., 2018

claim: Tail vane shape changes between species.
source: Tail vane shape changes through ontogeny (Bennett, 1995; O'Brien et al., 2018) and between species (Marsh, 1882; Döderlein, 1929; Frey et al., 2003), which underscores the importance of the tail vane in early pterosaur evolution.
evidence: Supported by citations to Marsh, 1882; Döderlein, 1929; Frey et al., 2003

claim: Tail vane shape variation underscores the importance of the tail vane in early pterosaur evolution.
source: Tail vane shape changes through ontogeny (Bennett, 1995; O'Brien et al., 2018) and between species (Marsh, 1882; Döderlein, 1929; Frey et al., 2003), which underscores the importance of the tail vane in early pterosaur evolution.

claim: Pterodactyloid pterosaurs evolved a shorter body plan with an anterior center of mass and large heads with cranial crests as the primary display structures.
source: As pterodactyloid pterosaurs evolved a shorter body plan with an anterior center of mass and large heads with cranial crests as the primary display structures (Jagielska and Brusatte, 2021), both the control and display functions of the tail were absorbed by the wings and head.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jagielska and Brusatte, 2021

claim: In pterodactyloid pterosaurs, both the control and display functions of the tail were absorbed by the wings and head.
source: As pterodactyloid pterosaurs evolved a shorter body plan with an anterior center of mass and large heads with cranial crests as the primary display structures (Jagielska and Brusatte, 2021), both the control and display functions of the tail were absorbed by the wings and head.
evidence: Inference supported by citation to Jagielska and Brusatte, 2021

claim: The cross-linked lattice suggests that the tail vane of early pterosaurs developed from a single contiguous structure rather than a combined structure of scales or feather-like integuments.
source: The cross-linked lattice recognised in this study suggests that the tail vane of early pterosaurs developed from a single contiguous structure rather than a combined structure of scales or feather-like integuments.

claim: The undulating vane edge might reflect an epidermal patterning.
source: While the undulating vane edge (Figure 2D) might reflect an epidermal patterning, the internal part of the tail vane was likely filled with connective tissue underneath the epidermal layer.

claim: The internal part of the tail vane was likely filled with connective tissue underneath the epidermal layer.
source: While the undulating vane edge (Figure 2D) might reflect an epidermal patterning, the internal part of the tail vane was likely filled with connective tissue underneath the epidermal layer.

claim: The medial part of the tail vane has a different tone under fluorescence compared to the lateral part.
source: The medial part of the tail vane, namely the periphery of the caudal vertebrae, has a different tone under fluorescence and the vertical structures lose clarity when compared to the lateral part of the tail vane (Figure 2A and B).

claim: The vertical structures lose clarity in the medial part of the tail vane when compared to the lateral part.
source: The medial part of the tail vane, namely the periphery of the caudal vertebrae, has a different tone under fluorescence and the vertical structures lose clarity when compared to the lateral part of the tail vane (Figure 2A and B).

claim: The different fluorescence tone potentially indicates a thicker subdermal connective tissue surrounding the caudal vertebrae.
source: This potentially indicates a thicker subdermal connective tissue surrounding the caudal vertebrae.

claim: The tail vane of pterosaurs consisted of bilateral fleshy folds on the end of the tail, comparable to the cetacean fluke that envelopes dense connective tissue.
source: Therefore, the tail vane of pterosaurs consisted of bilateral fleshy folds on the end of the tail, comparable to the cetacean fluke that envelopes dense connective tissue (Gavazzi et al., 2024).
evidence: Inference from observational data supported by citation to Gavazzi et al., 2024

claim: The growth series of the tail vane shape in Rhamphorhynchus muensteri begins with an extended teardrop/oval shape, becoming diamond-shaped, and eventually triangular.
source: The growth series of the tail vane shape in Rhamphorhynchus muensteri begins with an extended teardrop/oval shape, becoming diamond-shaped (Figure 2A and B), and eventually triangular (Bennett, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bennett, 1995 and observational data

claim: The three shapes of pterosaur tail vane development parallel the shape changes of the cetacean fluke during embryonic development.
source: These three shapes parallel the shape changes of the cetacean fluke during embryonic development (Stĕrba et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stĕrba et al., 2000

claim: It is possible that both the pterosaur tail vane and the cetacean fluke evolved through a shared developmental mechanism.
source: It is possible that both the pterosaur tail vane and the cetacean fluke evolved through a shared developmental mechanism, perhaps a co-option of the signaling pathway that drives appendage outgrowth (Gavazzi et al., 2024), eventually bringing about improved fluid dynamics of the limbs.
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citation to Gavazzi et al., 2024

claim: The shared developmental mechanism may be a co-option of the signaling pathway that drives appendage outgrowth.
source: It is possible that both the pterosaur tail vane and the cetacean fluke evolved through a shared developmental mechanism, perhaps a co-option of the signaling pathway that drives appendage outgrowth (Gavazzi et al., 2024), eventually bringing about improved fluid dynamics of the limbs.
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citation to Gavazzi et al., 2024
